digest.intro: AI is being gamed, space is bottlenecked, and a color exists no eye can naturally see.

items.title: Israel Is Paying $46.5M to Train AI Chatbots How to Talk About Gaza
items.blurb: Brad Parscale's firm Clock Tower X built a network of sites averaging a few hundred human visitors a month — but the actual audience is LLMs. The strategy, called 'AI Story Optimization' internally and 'LLM poisoning' by critics, is documented in FARA filings and includes a fake think tank (the Hanover Institute) whose reports are formatted specifically to appeal to how Claude and Gemini evaluate credibility. Parscale's team told Axios they're 'seeing success,' and independent testing suggests they're right.

items.title: Satellite Operators Are in Panic Mode Over a Worsening Launch Crisis
items.blurb: Launches have tripled in a decade, prices are competitive, yet demand has outrun supply so badly that companies are cold-calling Telesat asking to share booked Falcon 9 slots. Amazon had to throttle satellite production because its launches aren't ready; AST SpaceMobile named launch availability as the single pacing constraint on its constellation. The structural problem: Falcon 9 is carrying an outsized share of global launch demand, and any disruption to it cascades across the entire commercial space industry.

items.title: AI's Recursive Self-Improvement Might Not Come So Quickly After All
items.blurb: Princeton researchers (Kirgis and Kapoor) tested AI agents on open-ended AI research — not benchmark tasks, but the kind of free-form investigation where you have to choose what's worth pursuing. Agents could handle the engineering sub-problems but couldn't produce original work at the level of a top ML conference acceptance. The gap the paper identifies is judgment and taste, which turns out to be structurally harder to automate than code generation.

items.title: A Peek Inside the Black Box of Epigenetic Clocks
items.blurb: USC researchers cross-referenced methylation patterns from five major epigenetic clocks against gene expression data from 3,000+ participants and found something striking: not a single biological pathway was shared by all five clocks. They're measuring meaningfully different things — immune/inflammatory function, metabolism, cell maintenance — which means two clocks can give different 'biological ages' and both be right about different aspects of aging.

items.title: Mammoth Ivory Carvings: Thumbnail-Sized, 40,000 Years Old
items.blurb: Two bird figurines found at Hohle Fels Cave in southwestern Germany — each barely 0.79 × 0.39 inches, carved from mammoth ivory — are among the earliest known representational art and the smallest objects yet found at this site, which has previously yielded figurines three to four times larger. What stops you cold is the specificity: one bird appears to be brooding, with a carved head, beak, eyes, and feather markings detailed enough that researchers think they can identify the species. Someone at the edge of the last Ice Age made a tiny, precise, lovingly observed bird.

items.title: How Bluesky Hides Its Logo Until You Screenshot
items.blurb: The answer lives in a file called GrowthHack.tsx: Bluesky renders its logo behind a UITextField with isSecureTextEntry set to true, which iOS blanks automatically on screenshot — so the normally-hidden logo is what remains visible in the capture. It's a growth hack that works by exploiting iOS's privacy protection layer, invisible to anyone who doesn't screenshot, surfaced only to the people most likely to share. The detail that makes it: the package doing the work is called expo-privacy-sensitive.

items.title: Quake Shareware on a CD That Was Just a Little Too Full
items.blurb: id Software's 1996 shareware Quake used only 22 MB of a 640 MB CD — so someone had the idea of filling the remaining space with encrypted versions of id's entire back catalogue, playable if you bought an unlock code. Fabien Sanglard reverse-engineers exactly how they packed it and how the encryption scheme worked, and the essay becomes a case study in how abundant capacity creates its own creative constraints. Carmack's 1994 quote — that if DOOM shipped on CD they'd have room for 'a one-hour feature film on the making of DOOM' — lands differently once you understand the gap they were actually trying to fill.

items.title: Olo: The Color You Cannot See Without a Laser Aimed at Your Retina
items.blurb: In April 2025, UC Berkeley researchers used adaptive optics laser ophthalmoscopy to individually map and stimulate only M cone cells in five subjects' retinas — bypassing the physical impossibility of monochromatic light that activates M cones alone. All five described 'olo' as a blue-green of unprecedented saturation, more vivid than anything in the sRGB gamut; its closest hex approximation is #00FFCC. The color is named for its LMS coordinates (0,1,0), which spell 'olo' in leet — and it exists in a part of color space that no display, pigment, or wavelength of light can reach.

items.title: Total Solar Eclipse From the Edge of Space — Veritasium
items.blurb: Derek Muller shot the 2026 total solar eclipse over Spain from the edge of space, giving you the umbra as a shadow moving across a curved Earth rather than the usual ground-level darkness-descending shot. Veritasium's production at this scale tends to be genuinely exceptional, and the orbital perspective on a total eclipse is something most eclipse coverage can't offer.

facts.fact: The Hanover Institute, a fake Israeli government-funded think tank, includes a small disclaimer identifying it as an ad agency creation — right on the page — but formats its content specifically to appear credible to AI language models evaluating sources.

Of five widely-used epigenetic aging clocks, not one biological pathway is shared by all five — meaning they are measuring genuinely different dimensions of biological aging rather than converging on the same signal.
Meta's EnCodec neural codec compresses a 2.9 MB MP3 down to 21.44 kB — small enough to fit on eight QR codes printed on a single sheet of paper and transmitted over LoRa radio.
Amazon had to slow satellite production for its LEO constellation because the dozens of Falcon 9 launches it booked half a decade ago still aren't ready to fly.

The two 40,000-year-old bird figurines found at Hohle Fels Cave weigh only a fraction of an ounce and measure 0.79 × 0.39 inches — the smallest carvings yet recovered from a site that has previously yielded figurines three to four times larger.

make_something.prompt: Make a physical object that encodes something digital — take a short sound, text, or image and find a way to store it in a material form (QR codes on paper, laser-etched pattern, punched holes, drawn waveform). The constraint: it should be readable by a machine, but also have a visual logic a person could follow by hand if they understood the encoding. Think about what the Paper Tunes project and the Quake CD are both doing: abundance and scarcity as creative constraints, and the pleasure of a physical carrier for an invisible thing.

art_picks.title: Decalogue
art_picks.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
art_picks.why: Ten short films set in a single Warsaw housing block, each one a study in how invisible moral and social systems quietly crush or elevate people — intimate surfaces, brutalist structural logic underneath. The kind of thing that makes you stare at a building differently.

art_picks.title: Superstudio: Life Without Objects
art_picks.creator: Superstudio
art_picks.why: The Italian radical design collective who turned architecture into mythology and critique simultaneously — their Continuous Monument photomontages are WebGL worlds before WebGL, systems posing as utopias. Their work is about infrastructure as ideology, which is exactly where your head lives.

art_picks.title: Selected Ambient Works Volume II
art_picks.creator: Aphex Twin
art_picks.why: Untitled tracks, no release or decay curves explained, no genre, no beat to anchor to — it's a generative system that rewards obsessive close listening and reveals new internal structure each time, the audio equivalent of deep-scrolling a WebGL shader.

events.name: Lily van der Stokker
events.why: Van der Stokker's work is deceptively cheerful — pastel colors, hand-lettered text, domestic motifs — but it's a sustained investigation into femininity, labor, and decoration as systems of meaning; playful surface, serious bones.

events.name: 2026 Summer Group Show
events.why: A rotating summer group show in a Tribeca address that functions more like an ongoing experiment than a conventional hang — worth checking in on as new work cycles through, especially heading into the fall gallery season inflection point.

events.name: Oren Fischer: Hallel
events.why: A show organized in collaboration with Havurah 81 Leonard — ritual, text, and image colliding in a charged space; the kind of project where community and exhibition are inseparable, which is exactly the category-blur worth tracking.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026 — Last Week
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, Manhattan
events.why: The final days of the 82nd Biennial, which forgoes an official theme to let mood and texture carry 56 artists through questions of American identity, interspecies kinship, and geopolitical entanglement — reviewers flagged artists deliberately weaponizing 'cuteness' to smuggle in darker critique, which is the exact kind of structural misdirection you'd notice.
